q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "We discussed about the plan for an hour."
o: We discussed about the plan for an hour.
We discussed on the plan for an hour.
We have discussed about the plan for an hour.
We discussed the plan for an hour.
x: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes its object directly: we discuss a plan, not discuss about it or on it.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Please return back the book when you have finished it."
o: Please return the book when you have finished it.
Please return back the book when you have finished it.
Please return the book back when you have finished it.
Please return back the book when you will finish it.
x: 'Return' already means 'give back', so 'return back' is redundant. A time clause with 'when' also takes the present or present perfect, not 'will finish'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The prize was shared between Hamza and I."
o: The prize was shared between Hamza and me.
The prize was shared between Hamza and I.
The prize was shared between I and Hamza.
The prize was shared between myself and Hamza.
x: A pronoun after a preposition such as 'between' must be in the object form, 'me'. 'Myself' is reflexive and is used only when the subject is also 'I'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "She is living in Quetta since 2018."
o: She is living in Quetta since 2018.
She has been living in Quetta from 2018.
She lives in Quetta since 2018.
She has been living in Quetta since 2018.
x: An action that began in the past and continues now, marked with 'since' plus a point in time, needs the present perfect (continuous). 'From 2018' needs an end point such as 'to 2022'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "He found it hard to cope up with the pressure of the exam."
o: He found it hard to cope with the pressure of the exam.
He found it hard to cope up with the pressure of the exam.
He found it hard to cope up the pressure of the exam.
He found it hard to cope from the pressure of the exam.
x: The correct expression is 'cope with'. 'Cope up with' is a common error: there is no 'up' in this phrase.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "This road is more shorter than the old one."
o: This road is more shorter than the old one.
This road is shorter than the old one.
This road is shortest than the old one.
This road is more short than the old one.
x: A one-syllable adjective forms its comparative with '-er': 'shorter'. Adding 'more' to 'shorter' is a double comparative, and 'shortest' is a superlative, which cannot be followed by 'than'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The committee comprises of seven members."
o: The committee comprises of seven members.
The committee is consisting of seven members.
The committee consists of seven members.
The committee consists seven members.
x: 'Consist' needs 'of', but 'comprise' takes its object directly, so 'comprises of' is wrong. 'Consist' is a state verb and is not used in the continuous form.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "After lunch, Grandfather lays down for an hour."
o: After lunch, Grandfather lays down for an hour.
After lunch, Grandfather lie down for an hour.
Yesterday after lunch, Grandfather laid down for an hour.
After lunch, Grandfather lies down for an hour.
x: 'Lie' (lie, lay, lain) means to rest and takes no object; 'lay' (lay, laid, laid) means to put something down and needs an object. So he 'lies down' now, and yesterday he 'lay down', not 'laid down'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "I couldn't hardly hear the speaker."
o: I couldn't hardly hear the speaker.
I could not hardly hear the speaker.
I couldn't hardly heard the speaker.
I could hardly hear the speaker.
x: 'Hardly' is already negative in meaning, so adding 'not' makes a double negative. After 'could', the verb is the base form 'hear', not 'heard'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "When the bell rang, the students pack their bags and left the room."
o: When the bell rang, the students packed their bags and left the room.
When the bell rang, the students pack their bags and left the room.
When the bell rings, the students packed their bags and left the room.
When the bell rang, the students packed their bags and leave the room.
x: All three actions happened in the past, so all three verbs should be in the simple past: rang, packed, left. Mixing present and past forms breaks tense consistency.

q: Identify the error in this sentence: "He insisted to pay the bill although we had already paid it."
o: 'had already paid' should be 'already pays'
'the bill' should be 'a bill'
'insisted to pay' should be 'insisted on paying'
'although' should be 'despite'
x: 'Insist' is followed by 'on' plus a gerund: 'insisted on paying'. The past perfect 'had already paid' is correct for the earlier action, and 'despite' cannot introduce a full clause.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Scarcely had we reached the station than the train left."
o: Scarcely had we reached the station when the train left.
Scarcely had we reached the station than the train left.
Scarcely we had reached the station when the train left.
Scarcely had we reached the station then the train left.
x: 'Scarcely' at the start is followed by question order ('had we reached') and is paired with 'when'. 'Than' pairs with 'no sooner', not with 'scarcely'.

q: Which of these is a complete sentence?
o: Because the road was flooded.
Although the bus was late in the morning.
The flooded road near the old bridge.
The road was flooded, so the bus was late.
x: A complete sentence needs a main clause that can stand alone. Clauses beginning with 'because' or 'although' are dependent, and 'the flooded road near the old bridge' has no main verb.

q: Which option correctly fixes the run-on sentence "The lecture was long I fell asleep"?
o: The lecture was long, I fell asleep.
The lecture was long and, I fell asleep.
The lecture was long; I fell asleep.
The lecture was long I, fell asleep.
x: Two independent clauses can be joined by a semicolon. Joining them with only a comma creates a comma splice, which is still a run-on.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Walking to college, an accident was seen on the main road."
o: Walking to college, an accident was seen on the main road.
Walking to college, Sara saw an accident on the main road.
Walking to college, the accident happened on the main road.
While walking to college, an accident was seen by Sara on the main road.
x: An opening '-ing' phrase must describe the subject that follows it. Only Sara can be walking to college; in the other sentences the subject is 'an accident' or 'the accident', so the modifier dangles.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Ayesha likes reading, painting and to swim."
o: Ayesha likes reading, painting and to swim.
Ayesha likes reading, painting and swimming.
Ayesha likes to read, painting and swimming.
Ayesha likes reading, to paint and swim.
x: Items in a list should have the same grammatical form (parallel structure). Here all three are gerunds: reading, painting and swimming.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "He not only is clever but also hard-working."
o: He is not only clever but also hard-working.
He not only is clever but also hard-working.
He is not only clever but also works hard.
Not only he is clever but also hard-working.
x: 'Not only … but also' must join words of the same kind; here two adjectives, 'clever' and 'hard-working', both after 'is'. Starting a sentence with 'Not only' would need inversion ('Not only is he').

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "After finishing the experiment, the laboratory was cleaned."
o: After finishing the experiment, the laboratory was cleaned.
After finishing the experiment, the laboratory needed cleaning.
After finishing the experiment, cleaning the laboratory was done by the students.
After finishing the experiment, the students cleaned the laboratory.
x: The phrase 'after finishing the experiment' must be followed by whoever finished it, the students. In the other sentences the subject is the laboratory or 'cleaning', so the modifier dangles.

q: Which option correctly joins these words into one sentence: "When the results were announced. Everyone cheered."?
o: When the results were announced, everyone cheered.
When the results were announced; everyone cheered.
When the results were announced. Everyone, cheered.
When, the results were announced everyone cheered.
x: 'When the results were announced' is a dependent clause, a fragment on its own. It should be joined to the main clause with a comma, not a semicolon or full stop.

q: Which sentence places the modifier correctly?
o: The man sold me the watch with a grey beard.
The man with a grey beard sold me the watch.
With a grey beard, the watch was sold to me by the man.
The man sold the watch to me with a grey beard.
x: A modifier should sit next to the word it describes. 'With a grey beard' describes the man, so it must follow 'the man'; elsewhere it seems to describe the watch or me.

q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
o: The bus was late, however, we reached the hall in time.
The bus was late; however, we reached the hall in time.
The bus was late however we reached the hall in time.
The bus was late however, we reached the hall in time.
x: 'However' is not a joining word, so two full clauses linked by it need a semicolon before it and a comma after it. With only commas, the sentence is a comma splice.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The nurse checked his pulse, recorded his temperature and was giving him water."
o: The nurse checked his pulse, recorded his temperature and was giving him water.
The nurse checked his pulse, recording his temperature and gave him water.
The nurse checked his pulse, recorded his temperature and gave him water.
The nurse checked his pulse, recorded his temperature and giving him water.
x: The three actions form a series and should all be in the same form, the simple past: checked, recorded, gave.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The climate of Murree is cooler than Lahore."
o: The climate of Murree is cooler than Lahore.
The climate of Murree is cooler than those of Lahore.
The climate of Murree is cooler than that of Lahore.
The climate of Murree is more cooler than that of Lahore.
x: Like must be compared with like: the climate of Murree with the climate ('that') of Lahore, not with the city itself. 'Those' is plural, and 'more cooler' is a double comparative.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Being a rainy day, we stayed indoors."
o: Being a rainy day, we stayed indoors.
Being rainy, we stayed indoors.
It being a rainy day, so we stayed indoors.
As it was a rainy day, we stayed indoors.
x: 'Being a rainy day' would describe 'we', which makes no sense, so the modifier dangles. Adding 'so' after the absolute phrase 'It being a rainy day' leaves the sentence wrongly joined.

q: In formal written English, complete the sentence: "Each of the students ____ a laptop."
o: have
has
are having
were having
x: 'Each' is singular, so it takes a singular verb, 'has'. The plural noun 'students' after 'of' does not change this.

q: Neither the teacher nor the students ____ aware of the change.
o: was
were
is
has been
x: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject is 'the students', which is plural, so the verb is 'were'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Either my brothers or my father are going to collect me."
o: Either my brothers or my father is going to collect me.
Either my brothers or my father are going to collect me.
Either my brothers or my father have gone to collect me.
Either my brothers or my father were going to collect me.
x: With 'either … or', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. Here that is 'my father', which is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'is'.

q: One of the doctors in this hospital ____ from Peshawar.
o: are
were
have been
is
x: The subject is 'one', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'. 'Doctors' is part of the phrase 'of the doctors' and does not control the verb.

q: The captain, as well as his players, ____ happy with the result.
o: were
are
was
have been
x: A phrase introduced by 'as well as' does not add to the subject. The subject is 'the captain', which is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

q: In formal written English, complete the sentence: "Here ____ the results of the test."
o: is
has been
are
was
x: In a sentence beginning with 'here', the subject comes after the verb. The subject is 'the results', which is plural, so the verb is 'are'.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The quality of the mangoes have improved this year."
o: The quality of the mangoes have improved this year.
The quality of the mangoes has improved this year.
The quality of the mangoes are improved this year.
The quality of the mangoes were improving this year.
x: The subject is 'quality', which is singular; 'of the mangoes' only describes it. So the verb must be singular: 'has improved'.

q: Every boy and every girl ____ given a certificate.
o: was
were
are
have been
x: When two singular subjects joined by 'and' are each preceded by 'every' (or 'each'), the verb is singular. So the correct verb is 'was'.

q: Five hundred rupees ____ too much for this old book.
o: are
is
were
have been
x: An amount of money thought of as a single sum takes a singular verb, so 'five hundred rupees is too much'. The plural form of 'rupees' does not make the amount plural.

q: In formal written English, which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Neither of the two answers ____ correct."
o: are
is
were
have been
x: In formal English, 'neither' used as a pronoun is singular, meaning 'not one of the two'. So it takes the singular verb 'is'.

q: Not only the students but also the principal ____ invited to the ceremony.
o: were
have been
was
are
x: With 'not only … but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. That is 'the principal', which is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

q: Which of these sentences shows correct subject–verb agreement?
o: The news from the hospital is encouraging.
The news from the hospital are encouraging.
Mathematics are my favourite subject.
The scissors is on the table.
x: 'News' and 'mathematics' end in -s but are singular, so they take 'is'. 'Scissors' is plural and takes 'are'.

q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "The hostel provides ____ for two hundred students."
o: accomodation
accommodation
acommodation
accommadation
x: 'Accommodation' has a double 'c' and a double 'm', and an 'o' after the 'mm'.

q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "It is ____ to wash your hands before eating."
o: neccessary
necessery
necessary
nesessary
x: 'Necessary' has one 'c' and a double 's': ne-c-e-ss-ary. Its ending is '-ary', not '-ery'.

q: The doctor gave me some useful ____ about my diet.
o: advice
advise
advices
adviced
x: 'Advice' is the noun and is uncountable, so it has no plural 'advices'. 'Advise' is the verb, as in 'The doctor advised me'.

q: The new rule will ____ all the students of the college.
o: effect
affection
effective
affect
x: 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'to have an influence on'. 'Effect' is usually the noun (the result), and 'affection' and 'effective' are a noun and an adjective.

q: She spoke so ____ that everyone in the hall was moved.
o: emotional
emotion
emotions
emotionally
x: The blank describes how she spoke, so it needs an adverb, 'emotionally'. 'Emotional' is an adjective and 'emotion' is a noun.

q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "Power cuts are a daily ____ in summer."
o: occurence
ocurrence
occurrence
occurrance
x: 'Occurrence' has a double 'c', a double 'r' and ends in '-ence'. The 'r' doubles because 'occur' is stressed on its last syllable.

q: His ____ to help the flood victims surprised everyone.
o: willing
willingly
willingness
willed
x: The blank is the subject of the sentence, after 'his', so it needs a noun: 'willingness'. 'Willing' is an adjective and 'willingly' an adverb.

q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "He felt ____ when he forgot his lines on stage."
o: embarassed
embarrased
embarrassed
embbarassed
x: 'Embarrassed' has a double 'r' and a double 's'. Dropping one of the pairs is a very common mistake.

q: The ____ of the new bridge took three years.
o: construction
construct
constructive
constructed
x: After 'the' and before 'of', the sentence needs a noun: 'construction'. 'Construct' is a verb and 'constructive' an adjective.

q: The ____ of our college addressed the students on the first day.
o: principle
principality
principled
principal
x: 'Principal' means the head of a school or college. 'Principle' means a rule or belief, and 'principled' is an adjective.

q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "A ____ student checks every answer before handing in the paper."
o: conscientous
conscientious
consciencious
concientious
x: 'Conscientious' comes from 'conscience' and keeps its 'sc', with the ending '-tious'.

q: After the treatment, the patient's breathing became ____.
o: regularly
regularity
regulate
regular
x: 'Became' is a linking verb, so it is followed by an adjective describing the subject: 'regular'. An adverb such as 'regularly' cannot complete it.
